citation_details.title: Discovering Differences in Strategic Behavior Between Humans and LLMs
citation_details.author: Caroline Wang, Daniel Kasenberg, Kim Stachenfeld, Pablo Samuel Castro
citation_details.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in social and strategic scenarios, it becomes critical to understand where and why their behavior diverges from that of humans. While behavioral game theory (BGT) provides a framework for analyzing behavior, existing models do not fully capture the idiosyncratic behavior of humans or black-box, non-human agents like LLMs. We employ AlphaEvolve, a cutting-edge program discovery tool, to directly discover interpretable models of human and LLM behavior from data, thereby enabling open-ended discovery of structural factors driving human and LLM behavior. Our analysis on iterated rock-paper-scissors reveals that frontier LLMs can be capable of deeper strategic behavior than humans. These results provide a foundation for understanding structural differences driving differences in human and LLM behavior in strategic interactions.

citation_details.title: Collaborative rule learning promotes interbrain information alignment
citation_details.author: D. Moerel, T. Grootswagers, G. Quek, Sophie Smit, Manuel Varlet
citation_details.abstract: Social interactions shape our perception of the world, influencing how we interpret incoming information. Alignment between interacting individuals’ sensory and cognitive processes is key to successful cooperation and communication, but the neural processes underlying this alignment remain unknown. Here, we leveraged Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on electroencephalography (EEG) hyperscanning data to investigate information alignment in 24 pairs of participants who performed a categorization task together based on agreed-upon rules. Significant interbrain information alignment emerged within 45 ms of stimulus presentation and persisted for hundreds of milliseconds. Early alignment (45–180 ms) occurred in both real and randomly matched pseudo-pairs, reflecting shared sensory responses. citation_details.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
citation_details.author: Junyu Pan, Ruicheng Yin, Bao‐Liang Lu, Dongsheng Li, Wei-Long Zheng, Yansen Wang
citation_details.abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. citation_details.title: Context shapes action understanding in social interactions
citation_details.author: Johannes Keck, Kazuyuki Sato, Rouwen Cañal‐Bruland
citation_details.abstract: In social interactions, individuals anticipate what others are about to do next, enabling smooth social interactions and coexistence in daily life. Here, we examined how kinematic and contextual cues are weighted and integrated to predict an interactor's actions during dynamic, real-time competitive interactions. We analyzed 76 participants (38 dyads) freely playing 300 games of rock-paper-scissors each while tracking their kinematics using motion capture. Although movement kinematics consistently conveyed intention-related information, successful action selection depended primarily on how this information influenced predictions. Reinforcement-learning based contextual inference emerged as the strongest predictor of single-trial success and modulated the degree to which movement-derived predictions guided behavior. This study investigated the impact of music-induced positive emotion on the neural dynamics of decision-making in the Ultimatum Game. citation_details.title: A multibrain advantage for cooperative human behaviour
citation_details.author: Denise Moerel, Tijl Grootswagers, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet
citation_details.abstract: ABSTRACT Collaboration is a cornerstone of human behaviour, enabling individuals to achieve complex goals that transcend individual capabilities. While previous research has largely focused on the alignment of neural representations across brains during social interactions, real-world cooperation frequently involves complementary roles, where success depends on integrating distinct yet interdependent representations. Here, we combined electroencephalography (EEG) hyperscanning and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) methods to investigate neural representations in pairs of participants as they jointly performed a speeded two-dimensional visual matching task with asymmetric controls to encourage task division (i.e., attending to different stimulus features). citation_details.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors EEG classification dataset
citation_details.author: Raghu Vatsavai
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: This release provides a prepared EEG classification dataset derived from “Neural decoding of competitive decision-making in Rock-Paper-Scissors”, OpenNeuro ds006761, version 1.0.0, originally released under CC0 by Moerel and colleagues. The classification target is a player’s eventual choice of rock (rock), paper (paper) or scissors (scissors) from their decision-period EEG. The source contains 31 simultaneously recorded pairs comprising 62 players. Screening 29,760 player-trial candidates excludes 249 individual nonresponses, leaving 29,511 examples. A nonresponse excludes only the nonresponding player’s example; their opponent’s example remains eligible. Each example contains 64 scalp EEG channels and 512 samples at 256 Hz, expressed in volts. Preparation extracts the 2 second interval beginning at decision onset, excluding the response and feedback periods. Processing includes the source acquisition/player-bank correction, per-channel temporal centering, polyphase downsampling from 2,048 to 256 Hz, interpolation of the authors’ published bad channels and common average reference. Signals are stored at float32 precision. No additional bandpass filtering or automatic amplitude, ocular or muscle artifact rejection is applied. A pair-level random split with seed 42 produces 23,799 TRAIN examples from 25 pairs (50 players) and 5,712 TEST examples from six pairs (12 players). Both opponents and all their trials remain in the same partition. TRAIN contains 8,464 rock, 7,791 paper and 7,544 scissors examples; TEST contains 1,964 rock, 1,812 paper and 1,936 scissors examples. The release includes three files: RockPaperScissors_TRAIN.ts and RockPaperScissors_TEST.ts: signals and class labels in aeon format. RockPaperScissors_rows.tsv: row-aligned pair IDs, individual participant IDs, labels, source trial and sample coordinates, and optional grouped validation fold assignments. Five optional validation folds were constructed within TRAIN using StratifiedGroupKFold with random seed 42, keeping complete pairs together. TEST is excluded from these folds. The two signal files support the standard fixed TRAIN/TEST benchmark; the companion table enables pair-aware tuning and reporting of pair-wise classification metrics. Players choose different gestures across trials, so predictions should be evaluated per player-trial, optionally averaging performance across pairs. Both opponents must remain together during validation because their recordings arise from the same interaction. This single-trial classification task for unseen pairs differs from the source paper’s within-person analysis using aggregated trials. The participants and held-out pairs have been explored previously, so this release supports exploratory benchmarking rather than independent external validation. Published bad-channel flags are used for both TRAIN and TEST recordings, and potentially artifactual windows remain. Source dataset: OpenNeuro ds006761, version 1.0.0Source paper: Neural decoding of competitive decision-making in Rock-Paper-Scissors
